pages.title: A Mailbox on the Air
pages.text: The $(item)Packet BBS$() program turns the computer into a packet mailbox. Stations leave messages for each other and bulletins for everyone, and call in to read them when they like.$(br2)To host one, cable a $(l:radiocraft:computer/aprs)radio interface$() with a callsign to the computer and switch on a $(thing)VHF radio$() beside it, as for APRS. The mailbox answers the station's callsign with its own $(thing)SSID$(): W1BTR-1 by default.

pages.title: Calling In
pages.text: Callers send the mailbox $(thing)APRS messages$(), one command each: from an H19 terminal, the APRS program, an APRS handheld, or the BBS program's terminal page. The answers come back as messages.$(br2)$(li)? help$(li)L list, LM yours, LB bulletins$(li)R 12 read message 12$(li)SP W1ABC subject: send one$(li)SB ALL subject: a bulletin$(li)K 12 kill (yours only)$(li)B log off

After SP or SB the mailbox asks for a subject if you left it out, then takes the text a line per message until $(thing)/EX$(); $(thing)/AB$() gives up. A message holds up to 1000 characters; the mailbox up to 200 messages. A caller quiet for ten minutes is logged off and loses a half-written message.

pages.title: The Sysop
pages.text: At the hosting computer the SYSOP page lists every message and shows the traffic as it comes. Enter reads, N writes a message and B a bulletin from the station's callsign. Only the computer's owner (or an operator) may delete messages (Del) or change the SSID or take the mailbox off the air (F7).$(br2)The messages are kept on the computer's disk as BBS.DAT, so they go with the computer when it is picked up.

pages.title: Terminal
pages.text: Tab turns to the TERMINAL page, for calling someone else's mailbox from this computer. F7 sets its callsign (W1BTR-1); each line you type goes out as a message and its answers print below. Start with ? for its commands.$(br2)Packets can be lost on a weak path: if nothing comes back, send the line again.
A blank floppy and a chest.
